title: Anger Management
full_review:
Adam Sandler and Jack Nicholson make the latest odd-couple pairing in the displeasing comedy, "Anger Management" (Columbia).

A misunderstanding on an airline flight forces unassertive businessman Sandler to endure the attentions of volatile psychotherapist Nicholson.

Meek and underappreciated ad exec David finds himself sentenced to anger management behavior modification after a flight attendant and sky marshal misinterpret his actions. And, as luck would have it, his court-ordered therapist, Dr. Buddy Rydell, turns out to be the very guy who was the real troublemaker on the plane.

Group therapy with some rather scary individuals (including a bug-eyed John Turturro) is awful but then abrasive Buddy boldly moves right in with David to impose even more intensive therapy on his appalled subject. What could be worse? Well, Buddy's hitting on David's girlfriend, Linda (Marisa Tomei), might be the final straw that compels David to become the madman he's been assumed to be all along.

Director Peter Segal takes a reasonably funny premise -- a gentle soul tethered to a hot-tempered therapist -- but goes for cheap laughs involving transvestite hookers, making Buddhist monks turn to violence and jealous lesbians. The constant sexual references are at gutter level, and for a movie aimed at Sandler's target audience of impressionable pre-teen and teen males, the emphasis on how male anatomical size really matters is not a good -- or even funny -- message to send.

Sandler fills his role well compared to Nicholson, who looks uncomfortable in the sillier scenes, although a scene in which he smashes someone's car window clearly refers to Nicholson's own famously reported fit of anger against a motorist. As David's girlfriend, Tomei is a spunky, upbeat presence throughout the film, giving it some heart to balance out the frequent crude moments.

The story shows how David must learn to recognize his own inner rage and properly channel it, but some scenes, as when the Buddhist monks are deliberately provoked, can be interpreted as suggesting that violence is a good way to settle problems.

With its powerhouse male stars, "Anger Management" is likely headed for a big bite of the box office, but it's not a good choice for its target audience.

Due to some comically intended violence, continuous sexual references, brief same-sex kissing, an implied affair and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
